systeme-violent.place: Hôtel de Ville · the barricades of July 1830
text: « C'est votre système qui est violent, pas les lycéen·nes ! » — “It's your system that is violent, not the high-school kids!”, taped over the tags. Underneath, sprayed: NO WAR!, between stencilled rifles.
The question it asks is the oldest one in Paris: who is really violent, the street or the state?
scene: The word is Parisian. On 12 May 1588, the Day of the Barricades, Parisians rolled barrels (barriques) packed with earth and paving stones across the streets to stop Henri III's troops.
Then it came back, again and again: the Fronde in 1648, July 1830, June 1832, February and June 1848, the Commune in 1871, the Liberation in August 1944, the night of 10 May 1968 on rue Gay-Lussac.
systeme-violent.caption: Pinned where Paris fought in July 1830

art.commons: Eugène Delacroix - La liberté guidant le peuple.jpg
art.caption: Eugène Delacroix, Liberty Leading the People, 1830

text: « Vive la Commune » — “Long live the Commune”, hand-painted at the foot of a huge blind wall.
Shot in the 11th, a few minutes from Père-Lachaise, the cemetery where the Commune made its last stand.
scene: 18 March 1871: Paris refuses to hand its cannons over to the government and takes the city. For 72 days it runs itself: an elected council, church separated from state, night work banned in the bakeries.
It ends in the Bloody Week, 21–28 May. On 28 May, 147 fighters are shot against a wall in Père-Lachaise, the Mur des Fédérés, where the left still marches every spring.

art.commons: La Commune 1871. Barricade rue de Castiglione, 1er arrondissement, Paris. PH20145.jpg
art.caption: Barricade on rue de Castiglione, Paris Commune, 1871
art.credit: Attribué à Braquehais, Auguste Bruno (Dieppe, 18–01–1823 - La Celle-Saint-Cloud, 1875), photographe

autocollant-revolution.place: Around the 5th arrondissement · a green door
text: « Tu es communiste ? Rejoins-nous ! Révolution » — “Are you a communist? Join us! Revolution”. Someone has scrawled an answer across it: « Rebelle ? », “Rebel?”
A recruiting sticker. Its full-size posters are the next stop.
scene: In December 1920, at the Congress of Tours, most French socialists voted to join Lenin's Communist International. The French Communist Party was born.

By 1936 it was a mass party. The Popular Front won the elections, the factories went on strike, and workers won paid holidays and the 40-hour week. The marches ended at the Mur des Fédérés, as in the photo behind.

art.commons: Manifestation du Front populaire au mur des Fédérés - btv1b90282283.jpg
art.caption: Popular Front demonstration at the Communards' Wall, 1936
art.credit: Agence de presse Meurisse. Agence photographique (commanditaire)

autocollant-revolution.caption: Around the 5th · exact address not recorded

affiches-pcr.place: Around the 5th arrondissement · a shop shutter
text: The same « Tu es communiste ? Rejoins-nous ! », pasted four times over a shop shutter under a bearded portrait and the letters PCR, the Parti communiste révolutionnaire.
The men who wrote the answer to that question lived in Paris.
scene: Karl Marx lived here from 1843 to 1845, on rue Vaneau in the 7th. In August 1844 he met Friedrich Engels at the Café de la Régence, and their partnership began. France expelled him in early 1845.
Lenin lived here from 1908 to 1912, at 4 rue Marie-Rose in the 14th. Trotsky wrote for the anti-war paper Nashe Slovo from 1914 until France expelled him in 1916.

In July 1889, for the centenary of 1789, socialists meeting in Paris founded the Second International and made 1 May the day of workers' demonstrations. In April 1905, at the Salle du Globe, the French socialists united as the SFIO.

art.commons: Karl Marx by John Jabez Edwin Mayall 1875 - Restored.png
art.caption: John Mayall, Karl Marx, 1875

affiches-pcr.caption: Around the 5th · exact address not recorded

text: Pencilled under a Rue du Palais sign: « Macron castration ». Crude, personal, aimed at the body of the man in power.
Going after the ruler's body is a Paris tradition.
scene: In 1831 Charles Philipon, on trial in Paris for insulting King Louis-Philippe, sketched the royal face melting into a pear. La poire became the regime's nickname, drawn on walls all over the city.
Honoré Daumier went further: in Gargantua he drew the king as a giant swallowing the taxes of the poor. It earned him six months in prison.

art.commons: Honoré Daumier - Gargantua.jpg
art.caption: Honoré Daumier, Gargantua, 1831

text: « Une solution : révolution » — “One solution: revolution”, sprayed on a pink wall.
The rhyme works because everyone knows which revolution comes first.
scene: On 14 July 1789 Parisians stormed the Bastille for its gunpowder. Within weeks the feudal privileges were abolished and the Declaration of the Rights of Man was voted.
Every Paris uprising since has called itself a revolution or a sequel to one: 1830, 1848, 1871. The word on the wall carries all of them.

art.commons: Prise de la Bastille clean.jpg
art.caption: Jean-Pierre Houël, The Storming of the Bastille, 1789

text: « Nike la police »: « Nique la police », “Fuck the police”, spelled like the American sportswear brand.
Rage and logo in a single word.
scene: Paris has shouted at its police for a long time. In May 1968, after the riot police cleared the Sorbonne, the walls answered: « CRS = SS ».
In 2005, and again in June 2023, the deaths of teenagers during police encounters set off nights of rioting around Paris.

art.commons: Honoré Daumier, Rue Transnonain, le 15 avril 1834, 1834, NGA 6133.jpg
art.caption: Honoré Daumier, Rue Transnonain, 15 April 1834

louvre-galerie-apollon.place: Louvre Museum, door of the Galerie d'Apollon
text: Carved over the door: “The Louvre Museum, founded on 16 September 1792 by decree of the Legislative Assembly, was opened on 10 August 1793 by decree of the National Convention.”
A royal palace turned public museum, one year to the day after the monarchy fell.
scene: Behind this door: the French crown jewels.

On 19 October 2025, in broad daylight, thieves raised a furniture lift to a window of the Galerie d'Apollon and left with eight pieces of 19th-century crown jewellery in a few minutes. The Revolution opened the palace to everyone; the heist reminded everyone what is inside.

art.commons: Hubert Robert - The Grande Galerie - WGA19594.jpg
art.caption: Hubert Robert, The Grand Gallery of the Louvre, c. 1795

dessins-faits-main.place: 1st arrondissement, near Châtelet · an artists' collective
text: “Handmade drawings 25€”. One is captioned « Kill the past, embrace the future »: a man fires a pistol while kissing a woman, while another woman ignores them over cake.
Sold in an artists' collective near Châtelet, a short walk from the Louvre.
scene: “Kill the past” is the Futurist programme. On 20 February 1909 Filippo Tommaso Marinetti published the Futurist Manifesto on the front page of Le Figaro, in Paris: set fire to the libraries, flood the museums, worship speed.
Paris printed it, then ignored the advice. The Louvre is still standing next door.

art.commons: The City Rises by Umberto Boccioni 1910.jpg
art.caption: Umberto Boccioni, The City Rises, 1910

le-parisien.place: 15th arrondissement, off rue de la Convention
text: « Le moustique, ennemi public numéro 1 » — “The mosquito, public enemy number one”, across Le Parisien's front page, under a giant tiger mosquito.
The new public enemy is a few millimetres long, black with white stripes, and bites in broad daylight.
scene: The tiger mosquito was first found in mainland France in 2004, near Menton. It travels with us, in tyres, plant pots and car boots, and has since colonised Paris and the whole Île-de-France.
It can carry dengue, chikungunya and Zika, and Île-de-France has now recorded its first locally transmitted dengue cases. The tropics have arrived by commuter train.
le-parisien.note: « Ennemi public numéro un » is borrowed from 1930s America; France gave the title to the gangster Jacques Mesrine. Now it goes to an insect.

art.commons: CDC-Gathany-Aedes-albopictus-1.jpg
art.caption: James Gathany (CDC), tiger mosquito, Aedes albopictus

text: BIG BLACK COOK. Read it out loud. Now read it again, slower. Yes. They meant it.
A Black Caribbean restaurant in the 3rd that puts a dick joke on its sign has nothing to prove about its food.
scene: From 1963 to 1981 a state agency, the BUMIDOM, moved tens of thousands of people from Guadeloupe, Martinique, French Guiana and Réunion to mainland France, many into Paris jobs in hospitals, the post office and transport.
Their kitchens came with them. Accras, colombo and ti-punch are Paris classics now, and every summer the Tropical Carnival takes over the streets.
big-black-cook.caption: In the 3rd · exact address not recorded

text: Down in La Motte-Picquet–Grenelle: a purple card yelling « Own your money » in Grand Theft Auto lettering, for “the current account for your euros, bitcoins and stablecoins”.
Crypto sold like a heist game, on the same bevelled white tiles the métro has used since 1900.
scene: Upstairs is the old money: the Palais Brongniart, the stock exchange commissioned by Napoleon, and Avenue Montaigne, where the couture houses sell handbags priced like small cars.
Down here, the new pitch: be your own bank, hold your own coins, play money like a game. GTA gave you a city to rob. This ad sells you a way around the bank.

art.commons: Bourse de Paris, 3-4-1910 (Paris, 2e arrondissement) - btv1b6913935c.jpg
art.caption: Agence Rol, the Paris Bourse, 3 April 1910

text: In a bookshop window: Claude Ribbe's « Le Diable noir », “The Black Devil”, with General Thomas-Alexandre Dumas in full uniform on the cover.
Seen off rue de Grenelle, in the 7th, the district of ministries, the Invalides and the École militaire.
scene: Born in Saint-Domingue to a French nobleman and an enslaved woman, Dumas enlisted as a private in 1786. By 1793 he was a general commanding an army. Only a revolution could promote a Black man that fast.
Then France turned back. Bonaparte sidelined him after Egypt and restored slavery in 1802. Dumas died poor in 1806.

Paris carried the line on. His son became the most-read novelist in France. Gaston Monnerville, born in Cayenne, presided over the upper house from 1947 to 1968. Félix Éboué entered the Panthéon in 1949, Alexandre Dumas in 2002.
le-diable-noir.note: The general's statue on place Malesherbes was melted down during the Occupation. Today a pair of giant broken shackles stands in its place.

art.commons: Thomas-Alexandre Dumas.jpg
art.caption: General Thomas-Alexandre Dumas

text: A bronze medallion of Stendhal on a stone column in the Luxembourg garden; the plaque credits Auguste Rodin, after David d'Angers. Green streaks run down the stone where the bronze weeps in the rain.
scene: Paris writers worked on foot. Walking was how they gathered faces, rumours and impressions; Baudelaire made the flâneur a hero of modern life, and Walter Benjamin made him a theory.

Stendhal knew his own generation would not read him. The Red and the Black and The Charterhouse of Parma sold poorly; Balzac was nearly alone in praising him. He wrote that he would be understood around 1880, and that he held a lottery ticket whose prize was to be read in 1935.
He collapsed on a Paris street in 1842 and died the next day, almost unknown. Both dates came true. Every artist in this city makes the same bet.

art.commons: Portrait de Stendhal en 1840, 88.23.jpg
art.caption: Portrait of Stendhal in 1840

graffitis-zero.place: Jardin du Luxembourg · the public toilets
text: Inside the toilets of the Jardin du Luxembourg: a big blue ZERO, and around it « Free Gaza », « Free Palestine », « Mélenchon 2027 », « Nik la police », « Qui pour nous protéger de la police ? », “Who will protect us from the police?”.
The Senate sits in the palace at the end of the garden. The angriest wall in the park is a few hundred metres from the upper house of Parliament.
scene: In 2023 the pension reform was forced through without a vote, under article 49.3, after months of strikes. In 2024 the president dissolved the Assembly: the far right won the first round, a hastily formed left alliance the second, and the centre clung on between them.
Governments have fallen one after another since. This wall is the country in miniature: young, furious, split between left and right, and united against the middle.

art.commons: Umberto boccioni, rissa in galleria, 1910, 01.jpg
art.caption: Umberto Boccioni, Riot in the Galleria, 1910

text: « Forza Napoli » on a blue banner over a small Italian restaurant, the windows covered in the club's colours.
scene: Napoli won its first Italian title in 1987 with Diego Maradona, then again in 1990, 2023 and 2025. In Naples, Maradona is a saint; in Paris, the shrine is a restaurant window.
Italians came to Paris in large numbers from the late 19th century, and brought their cafés with them, like the Café Napolitain on the boulevards, behind.

art.commons: Béraud - Le boulevard des Capucines, le soir, devant le Café Napolitain, Vers 1880.jpg
art.caption: Jean Béraud, In Front of the Café Napolitain, c. 1880

forza-napoli.caption: In the 15th · exact address not recorded

abribus-burger-king.place: A bus shelter · exact spot not recorded
text: Burger King's « Ice Burger », ice cream in a bun dripping chocolate, and the line « Un ovni parmi les desserts », “A UFO among desserts”.
For once an ad tells the truth: an alien object, landed in the capital of pastry.
scene: Paris invented the art poster. In the 1890s Jules Chéret, then Mucha and Toulouse-Lautrec, turned ads for drinks and cabarets into lithographs people peeled off the walls to keep. Same job, selling, done by hand, by masters.

Burger King came to France in 1980, left in 1997, and returned in December 2012 at Gare Saint-Lazare, to queues hours long. In the city of haute cuisine, the American fast-food giant now owns the bus shelters.

art.commons: Apéritif Mugnier affiche, Jules Chéret 90.jpg
art.caption: Jules Chéret, poster for Apéritif Mugnier

feu-vert.place: Near the Madeleine · a protest march
text: « USA Champions », across the back of a man's jacket, crossing on the green light.

Taken during one of the recent national protest days. Thousands marching against the system, and on one back, without irony, the name of the system's winner. Behind them, police on a polished Haussmann street.
scene: American troops paraded down the Champs-Élysées on 29 August 1944, four days after the Liberation. Then came Marshall Plan dollars, Coca-Cola, Hollywood, jeans, and in 1992 Disneyland, at the city's door.

France built itself as the exception: it left NATO's integrated command in 1966 and still defends a “cultural exception” for its films and songs. And the most ordinary jacket at an anti-system march still says USA.
feu-vert.note: Caillebotte's Paris Street; Rainy Day, behind, may be the most Parisian street painting there is. It hangs in the Art Institute of Chicago.

art.commons: Gustave Caillebotte - Paris Street; Rainy Day - Google Art Project.jpg
art.caption: Gustave Caillebotte, Paris Street; Rainy Day, 1877

feu-vert.caption: Near the Madeleine · exact spot not recorded

text: « Gospel Dream — chants authentiques de l'église afro-américaine », “authentic songs of the African-American church”: a choir in purple robes, in concert at the Église Saint-Louis-d'Antin, Friday 1 May, 8:30 pm.
scene: Paris churches have always been concert halls. Around 1200, Léonin and Pérotin at Notre-Dame wrote some of Europe's first great polyphony, four voices at once, under vaults still being built.
Then came the organs: Widor at Saint-Sulpice for 64 years, Saint-Saëns and then Fauré at the Madeleine, Messiaen at La Trinité for six decades. Tonight the same stone carries a gospel choir.

art.commons: Pérotin - Viderunt omnes.jpg
art.caption: Pérotin, Viderunt omnes, Notre-Dame school, c. 1198

gospel-dream.caption: In the 7th · exact spot not recorded

text: « Le Parc de l'Étrange », “The Park of the Strange”, “the immersive Halloween event”, on a black banner at the gate of Parc André-Citroën.
Read it twice. L'étrange is the strange, the uncanny. Add one letter and l'étranger is the stranger, the foreigner, the immigrant. Paris has always been both.
scene: Under the city lie the Catacombs: from 1786, the bones of some six million Parisians were moved from overflowing cemeteries into the old quarries. The capital literally stands on its dead.

Jung and Mircea Eliade wrote about the axis mundi, the centre where heaven, earth and the underworld meet. Paris works like one. People are drawn here from everywhere, the world changes here, and every layer is both a weight and a step: we stand on the shoulders of giants, and on their bones.

art.commons: Nadar - Catacombes de Paris - NPS 74.jpg
art.caption: Nadar, Catacombs of Paris, 1861–1862

text: « À nos morts », “To our dead”: the war memorial of the 15th. Stone figures crowd the steps on either side; in the middle, one stands with an arm stretched out.
Behind them, Danton and Robespierre look on, enlisted in the defence of the Republic.
scene: About 1.4 million French soldiers died in the First World War, and millions more came home wounded. Disabled veterans led the victory parade on 14 July 1919. Every memorial is a haunted house: names for bodies that never came back.

Would the men of 1793 have signed up? Robespierre fought the war of 1792 at the Jacobin Club: “No one loves armed missionaries.” Danton called for audacity to save the Republic, then tried to negotiate peace. Neither would obviously have blessed a war of empires allied with the Tsar.

art.commons: Maréchal Ferdinand Foch saluant du bâton, à cheval, 14 juillet 1919.jpg
art.caption: Marshal Foch at the Victory Parade, 14 July 1919

text: A yellow Citroën 2CV with « 007 » on the door and stick-on bullet holes, a replica of the car Bond escapes in in For Your Eyes Only (1981).
Parked in the park built on the old Citroën factory site. The humblest car in France turned spy car.
scene: Paris sells elegance to the world, and the world comes here to negotiate. The 1919 Peace Conference redrew Europe from the Quai d'Orsay; the Paris Peace Accords of 1973 ended America's direct war in Vietnam; the Paris climate agreement was sealed at Le Bourget in 2015.
UNESCO and the OECD are headquartered here, and NATO was until 1967. Bond came for the glamour, and for the spies.

art.commons: Orpen, William (Sir) (RA) - The Signing of Peace in the Hall of Mirrors, Versailles, 28th June 1919 - Google Art Project.jpg
art.caption: William Orpen, The Signing of Peace in the Hall of Mirrors, 1919
